Wind is a substantial factor. Reading the wind and adjusting for it are primary skills for long-range shooters.

The effect that wind has on a projectile is dependent on both time of flight through the windy area, and the size and shape of the bullet in question. If you are shooting a centerfire rifle or pistol at 25 yards, the effect is quite small because the time of flight is so short. If you are taking a handgun out to fifty yards or a rifle out past a hundred, wind is increasingly likely to be a factor. Of course the size of the target matters too - hitting a dime at a hundred yards is a much more delicate operation than hitting a deer at the same range.

If the wind were steady and consistent there would be no limit to your ability to adjust for it. In real life, wind is tricky, not only gusting and slowing, but changing direction too. What's worse is that it's not uncommon to have different winds, perhaps blowing in different directions, between you and the target when long ranges are involved. 1000 yard shooters deal with this sort of thing all the time.

This document suggests that a 10mph wind, at 90 degrees to the shooter, would account for a 6MOA drift with a .308 match bullet:

http://www.millettsights.com/downloads/jeffhoffmanwindformula.pdf

6MOA basically means six inches of drift at 100 yards, 12 inches at 200 yards, and so on.

Shot competitively at 600 and (less often) 1000 and can confirm that after missing left by a number of inches and compensating, a sudden change in wind from ~5mph left to ~5mph right can push you totally off paper. It's fucking intimidating to make an adjustment and suddenly if you weren't paying attention to the flags you have absolutely no idea where that shot went. I always shot relatively light .243 ackley improved or 6mmbrx so that definitely contributed to the winds ability to bully me off target.

Ballistic physics, man.

The technically-correct and short answer is "as much as wind affects the course of every projectile."

The useful answer is "not very much at short ranges because bullets move very, very fast, and get to their targets before the wind has had time to move them much."

But at longer ranges - which 400 yards most definitely qualifies as - yeah, wind's a factor. It'll move the bullet as much as a crosswind on a bullet-sized thing would move such a thing in the time it takes for the bullet to travel 400 yards.

Blathering

PROTIP: When asking several questions, go for the numbered list, not the bulleted list, so people can answer by number. But then again, bulleted list in /v/guns... I'm torn.

Do you ever have to account for wind if you're firing at <25 yards?

No.

Even if you are shooting something relatively slow - like a 100-grain, .380 ACP Handgun round which clocks in under the speed of sound - it'll still be travelling over 900 feet per second. So let's use 900 feet per second on a 100-grain projectile.

At 25 yards (75 feet), the bullet will take 1/12th of a second, or 0.083 seconds, to reach the target.

Gravity will accelerate the projectile downward at ~32.2 feet/second2... for a total drop of 0.111 feet, or around 1.3 inches.

Before we try to figure out the effect that a (cross-) wind would have, stop and think about what kind of wind you'd need, blowing upwards, to counteract gravity in general. Do we ever really see that in real life? Not really... but imagine there's a wind blowing that's accelerating things upward enough that shit don't fall down anymore - you drop a bullet out of your hand and it just floats in the air, the updraft is so strong.

Now turn that wind sideways... and it'll move the bullet 1.3 inches off-target at 25 yards.

How strong does wind speed have to get in order for it to be generally considered to be impossible to shoot? (again, this probably changes with distance and maybe bullet-type)

Depends (primarily) on how far away the target is, and how fast your bullet's moving to begin with.

Bullets leave the muzzle at much more than their terminal velocity, and begin slowing down immediately. At short ranges (such as <25 yards in the first question), you can mostly ignore this effect since the bullet will reach its target before it's slowed significantly.

The reality, though, is that every foot the bullet travels will take longer to cover than the previous foot, and this starts to add up the farther you're shooting - the bullet will take longer to travel from 300 yards to 301 yards, than it did to travel from 0 yards to 1 yard.

As a result, there is more time in the air for both gravity and wind to affect the bullet and the bullet will shear down and to the side more for every foot traveled than it did for each previous foot of forward travel. This will stop when the projectile reaches its terminal velocity, but you're realistically never going to reach that point on a shot that was intended to hit.

The closer your target, the less-pronounced this effect. The faster your bullet, the less-pronounced this effect.
